lead: A signal carries information as a function of an independent variable. A system takes an input signal and produces an output signal. In continuous time the variable is a real number t, usually seconds. In discrete time it is an integer n, a plain count with no unit. Every phone, ECG monitor and power grid runs on this pair: measure a signal, pass it through a system, read the result. This chapter fixes the words and the notation x(t), x[n], y(t) and y[n] that the rest of the subject uses.
prereq: You need: basic trigonometry (sin and cos at standard angles such as π/2 and π) and the school idea of a function; no earlier chapter of this book.

sections.h3: A signal is a function that carries information

blocks.text: A signal is a function of an independent variable that carries information. Write x(t). Here x is the signal, t is the independent variable, and the number x(t) at one particular t is the amplitude. The amplitude carries units: volts on a microphone lead, amperes in a motor winding, °C in a room, rupees for a share price. Some syllabi call a signal a function of one or more independent variables; a photograph has two, row and column.

A continuous-time (CT) signal has a value for every real t in its range. Speech voltage from a microphone is CT: between t = 0.001 s and t = 0.0011 s there are infinitely many instants, and a voltage exists at each one.

A discrete-time (DT) signal has a value only at integer n. Write x[n]. The number n is a count, not a time: n = …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … Nothing is defined at n = 2.5. Each value x[n] is called a sample, whether it was measured, counted or computed from a formula.

items: Daily closing price of one share on a stock exchange: one value per trading day, index n = 0, 1, 2, …
Number of UPI transactions completed each day: discrete by nature, no sampling needed.
Room temperature read by a sensor every 10 ms: discrete in the record, though the room itself is continuous.

blocks.where: x(t) is the CT signal; T<sub>s</sub> is the sampling interval in seconds; n is the integer index; x[n] is the resulting sequence. This equality holds only for ideal sampling.

sections.h3: A system maps an input signal to an output signal

blocks.text: A system is an operator that turns an input signal into an output signal. Write y(t) = T{x(t)} for CT and y[n] = T{x[n]} for DT. T is the rule, x is the input, y is the output. Input and output share the same independent variable.

Treat the system as a black box. What matters is the rule from input to output, not the circuit inside. The box may be an op-amp board, a few lines of Python, or a physical room whose temperature reacts to a heater. Chapter 1.5 classifies CT and DT systems in detail.

Two examples fix the idea. An audio amplifier with y(t) = 100 x(t) takes an input of 20 mV and gives 2 V. A moving average that replaces each reading by the mean of the last five readings is a DT system: input x[n], output y[n], index n in both.

items: Read the independent variable on the input. Real t in seconds means CT; integer n means DT.
Check that the output uses the same variable. A CT input with a DT output, such as a sampler, makes a hybrid system: it converts CT to DT, so it is neither a pure CT nor a pure DT system.
State the rule T in one line, then test it. Samplers and reconstruction are studied with the sampling theorem.

sections.h3: CT and DT side by side

head: Continuous time
Discrete time
rows: t, a real number in seconds
n, an integer with no unit
sampler output, per-day count, log file

blocks.text: Discrete-time signals are not always sampled. Transactions per day and the daily close of a stock are discrete before any instrument touches them. Sampling is one way to make a DT signal, not the definition of it. The sampling theorem states how much of x(t) survives the sampler.

The two families need different tools. CT signals are analysed with the Fourier series, Fourier transform and Laplace transform (see Fourier series and Fourier transform, and Laplace transform analysis). DT signals use the DTFT, DFT and Z-transform. All of them build on the notation fixed here.

examples.question: A vibration sensor on a pump gives the voltage x(t) = 4 sin(20πt) V with t in seconds. A sampler records it every T<sub>s</sub> = 10 ms, producing x[n] = 4 sin(0.2πn) V. (a) Say which signal is CT and which is DT. (b) Show that sampling x(t) every 10 ms gives the stated x[n]. (c) Compute x(0.025 s) and x[5], each in volts.
steps: (a) x(t) is defined for every real t in seconds, so it is CT. x[n] is defined only at integer n, so it is DT.
(b) Sampling means x[n] = x(nT<sub>s</sub>), with T<sub>s</sub> = 10 ms = 0.01 s.
20π × 0.01 = 0.2π rad, so x[n] = 4 sin(20π × 0.01 n) = 4 sin(0.2πn) V. This matches the given sequence.
examples.answer: x(t) is a CT signal and x[n] is a DT signal; x(0.025 s) = 4 V and x[5] = 0 V.
examples.check:
import math
x_at_0025 = 4 * math.sin(20 * math.pi * 0.025)
x_at_index_5 = 4 * math.sin(0.2 * math.pi * 5)
print(round(x_at_0025, 6))
print(round(x_at_index_5, 6))

traps: x[n] is not x(nT<sub>s</sub>) in general. That equality needs ideal sampling; n is an integer count, never a time in seconds.
Brackets and parentheses are not decoration: x(t) is CT, x[n] is DT. Writing x(5) for a sequence loses marks.
The argument of sin and cos is in radians. 0.5π rad is 90°, not 0.5°; a calculator left in degree mode gives wrong answers.
A system is CT or DT by the variable on its input and output, not by its hardware. A filter running on a phone is still a DT system.
x(t) is the whole function; x(2) is one number. Saying 'the signal is 4 V' describes one amplitude, not the signal.

quiz.q: Define a signal and a system. What is the independent variable in each of x(t) and x[n]?
quiz.a: A signal is a function of an independent variable that carries information. A system is an operator that maps an input signal to an output signal. In x(t) the independent variable is real t, usually seconds; in x[n] it is the integer index n, which has no unit.

quiz.q: Why is a discrete-time signal x[n] not defined at n = 2.5?
quiz.a: n is an index, not a time. The sequence holds one value per integer index only. A value at n = 2.5 would need a point between the second and third sample, and no such point exists in a DT signal.

quiz.q: A sequence is x[n] = 3 cos(0.25πn) V. Find x[0], x[2] and x[4], with units.
A CT signal is x(t) = 10 sin(100πt) mV. Find x(0.005 s).
Give one example of a DT signal that was never produced by sampling a CT signal, and explain why it is DT.
quiz.a: The number of UPI transactions completed each day. One count exists per day and nothing exists between days, so the independent variable is an integer day index. There is no half-day transaction count to sample.

quiz.q: A student claims every DT signal comes from sampling a CT signal. Test the claim and state what it implies for the order of study.
quiz.a: The claim is false: per-day counts and daily prices are discrete by nature, and a sequence can be defined by a formula such as x[n] = 3 cos(0.25πn) with no CT parent. Sampling is one route to a DT signal. So DT signals are studied as a type in their own right, and the sampling theorem is a link between the two types, not a definition of DT.

quiz.q: A sensor output x(t) in volts passes through a sampler and then a moving-average block. Name the input and output of the moving average and say whether it is a CT or DT system. Justify.
quiz.a: The moving average takes x[n] in volts and gives y[n] in volts. Its input and output are both indexed by integer n, so it is a DT system. The sampler before it is a hybrid system: its input is CT and its output is DT.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry rarely starts from x(t): a sensor node samples at a fixed rate and ships x[n] to a server, so the DT view is the working view in IoT and telecom. Machine learning on time series treats the index n as the row number of a table, and the model never sees t. Radar, speech recognition and ECG monitors all pair a CT front end with a DT back end. Search next for data acquisition system, Nyquist rate and time series sampling.
